SAN DIEGO...WESTERN RIVERSIDE AND SOUTHWESTERN SAN BERNARDINO
COUNTIES...


...UPDATED AVIATION DISCUSSION FOR 12Z TAF ISSUANCE...

As of 12:30 AM local time, a few low clouds were covering parts of 
coastal San Diego County. Perhaps some very localized fog exists 
where clouds and terrain are intersecting, reducing visibility's 
below 1 mile. Nearly 800 nautical miles to the southwest, 
Tropical Storm Rachel has begun its turn northeastward moving at 
less than 10 miles per hour. Its path will have a significant 
influence on the upcoming weather as its remnants and surface low 
pressure approach the west coast of North America. 

Temperatures...Today marks the last day of significant heat 
(especially in the low deserts) before a significant pattern change 
to the region, regardless of the tropical activity. What is most 
certain in this forecast is that temperatures are bound to cool off 
significantly into early next week. Highs today fall a few degrees 
from yesterday - 80s coastal / mid-90s inland / 100s low desert - as 
a closed upper low and broad west coast trough dip into California. 
Broad cloud coverage from Rachel's remnants during the day Saturday 
drop highs around 10 degrees from Friday. The trough continues to 
deepen Sunday, dropping highs another 5-10 degrees and then finally 
the trough axis moves over SoCal on Monday, bringing the coolest 
temperatures some areas have seen since last April. The current 
forecast has high temperatures Monday in the mid/upper 60s across 
the coastal basin and high deserts with highs in the 40s in the 
mountains and 70s in the low deserts. If the closed low positions 
itself over Socal instead of the Great Basin as the GFS is showing, 
we could see 700mb temperatures around -5 C and highs could be even 
a few degrees cooler than forecast. Minimum temperatures are also 
expected to drop a few degrees each night inland, from around 70
this morning to around 50 for early Tuesday (and to the upper 50s
at the coast).

Rainfall...Tropical Storm Rachel approaches the coast this weekend, 
bringing a chance for an initial soaking rain Sunday. The broader 
trough very slowly moves through Monday with its own moisture and 
mid-level vorticity from the trough axis could bring another round 
of showers Monday into Tuesday. The first wave comes from TS 
Rachel, which is timing periodic rainfall between 1 AM-5 PM 
Sunday. While there isn't much background instability (almost no 
CAPE), PWAT's will generally range from 1.3-1.8 inches (>2 inches 
for high end scenario) and the surface low could generate periods 
of persistent moderate rainfall with rain rates over 0.5 in/hr in 
the mountains. Rainfall amounts from TS Rachel will largely depend
on its track, especially for some of the mountain areas. If the 
surface low from TS Rachel landfalls farther south (>100 miles 
south of SD) and it continues to track east, the amount of 
rainfall especially in the coastal basin and desert slopes would 
be very limited as there is initially not much instability to 
generate rain. Based on NBM probabilities, this scenario 
represents around 25% of solutions, yielding to rainfall less than
0.25" for the entire coastal basin and less than 0.10" for areas 
farther west like Orange County. The most likely scenario, 
accounting for around 50% of solutions, brings the coastal 
basin/deserts a soaking rain between 0.25-1" during this first 
wave with 1-2 inches in the mountains. Assuming the low tracks 
close enough to the mountains, easterly flow over the desert 
slopes could yield surprisingly high rates (>0.5/hr) and totals 
(1-2 inches). The higher end case (~25% chance) brings 1- 2" over 
the coastal basin/deserts and 2-4" over the mountains, which could
result in more numerous impacts across the region. The remnants 
of TS Rachel should move out of the region quickly Sunday evening,
yielding breaks in rainfall. The following waves of showers 
Monday and Tuesday will be driven by the upper level dynamics of 
the trough and will feature a much drier airmass. Totals 
Monday/Tuesday should look more similar to a light wet season 
system: 0.10-0.25" for the coastal basin, higher amounts in the 
mountains and less than 0.10" for desert communities. Since the 
trough will drive in much colder air, light snow accumulations are
possible with this second round above 8,000 feet.

Winds...There is similar uncertainty with the winds. A track farther 
southeast would yield to much lighter winds gusting below 20 mph 
through the coastal basin while the most likely scenario (~50% 
chance) that the surface low makes a close approach yielding to wind 
gusts 20-40 mph through the coastal basin, with gusts 50-70 mph in 
the mountains and passes during the day Sunday. Winds remain onshore 
Monday but much less strong than Sunday.
